Technical details of prespecified endpoint horizons

Graeme L. Hickey

Source: vignettes/endpoint-horizons-technical.Rmd
endpoint-horizons-technical.Rmd

The endpoint-horizon functions allow the endpoint time to change according to a prespecified schedule, conditional on the trial reaching each interim look. The success calculation uses the endpoint assigned to that look. The futility calculation predicts success at the eventual maximum-sample-size endpoint. When these endpoints differ, their predictive models use separate follow-up data cuts.

This vignette describes the statistical calculations and their implementation in sim_horizon_trials(), sim_horizon_paths(), and apply_horizon_rules(). Extending an endpoint from 12 to 18 months provides a worked example. The technical details of the Goldilocks design cover the underlying fixed-horizon methods.

Design specification

Let the interim enrollment sizes be n_1 < \cdots < n_L < N_{\max}, with success endpoint times H_1 \le \cdots \le H_L \le H_F. Here, H_F is the endpoint for the maximum-N final analysis and for every futility prediction. All participants have planned outcome collection through H_C \ge H_F from enrollment, including participants recruited before the endpoint changes.

Quantity R argument Interpretation
n_\ell, H_\ell endpoint_schedule Data frame with columns N and horizon; one row per interim
N_{\max} N_total Maximum enrollment; not an additional interim look
H_F final_horizon Maximum-N endpoint and futility prediction horizon
H_C followup_horizon Planned collection duration for each participant
Supported endpoint times endpoint_horizons Horizons evaluated and retained by sim_horizon_paths()
Dropout reference time dropout_horizon Time at which prop_loss specifies the dropout probability

The schedule is applied before evaluating each reached look. It does not use an interim estimate or predictive probability to choose whether to extend the endpoint. A terminal stopping decision prevents later scheduled changes from taking effect. If the trial continues to maximum enrollment, its final analysis uses H_F after endpoint ascertainment; reaching N_{\max} does not itself trigger an interim analysis.

Two data cuts at the same calendar date

Let E_i be enrollment time, T_i the event time from enrollment, and D_i the independent dropout time. The calendar date of look \ell is t_\ell = E_{n_\ell}. For an enrolled participant and an analysis horizon H, the available data are

X_{i\ell}(H) = \min\{T_i, D_i, H, t_\ell-E_i\}, \qquad \delta_{i\ell}(H) = I\{T_i \le \min(D_i,H,t_\ell-E_i)\}.

The success data set uses H=H_\ell; the futility data set uses H=H_F. Participants not yet enrolled contribute no observed events or exposure to either model. Their outcomes are generated only for the maximum-N prediction. The implementation gives a participant enrolled exactly at the look a negligible positive exposure to accommodate the survival calculations.

For example, an event at month 15 is represented as event-free administrative censoring at month 12 in a 12-month success calculation. It can enter an 18-month futility calculation only if month 15 has already been reached at that participant’s current follow-up. A dropout at month 15 does not make the 12-month endpoint missing. A dropout at month 8 leaves the outcome after month 8 unobserved in both calculations.

Figure 1. Separate success and futility predictions. When the current and final horizons are equal, the data cuts coincide and the predictions share one fitted hazard model. When they differ, fitting one model to the longer data cut and changing only the endpoint of the completed-data analysis would allow late follow-up to inform early success; the implementation therefore fits each data cut separately.

Predictive hazard models and completed-data analyses

Gamma updating within each data cut

The analysis model has piecewise-constant hazards \lambda_{zj} for arm z and interval j, with independent shape-rate priors

\lambda_{zj} \sim \operatorname{Gamma}(a_{zj}, b_{zj}).

For a given look and horizon H, let d_{zj\ell}(H) and y_{zj\ell}(H) be the event count and total exposure in the interval after applying both the calendar and endpoint cuts. With empty_interval = "prior", the predictive posterior is

\lambda_{zj}\mid\mathcal D_\ell(H) \sim \operatorname{Gamma}\{a_{zj}+d_{zj\ell}(H),\ b_{zj}+y_{zj\ell}(H)\}.

cutpoints defines the master analysis partition. At horizon H, only cutpoints strictly less than H are retained, and the last interval ends at H. The corresponding leading columns of the interval-specific priors are retained in the same order. A cutpoint equal to H does not create an interval beyond the endpoint. Later intervals and their priors are not combined with earlier ones.

An interval with no observed exposure remains governed by its own prior under the default policy. This can matter substantially for the longer-horizon futility calculation at early looks. The other available policies are "propagate", the existing adjacent-interval heuristic, and "error". Bayesian piecewise-exponential designs discusses predictive and analysis priors in more detail.

Predictive completion and success scores

For each of the M= N_impute posterior draws, the success calculation imputes outstanding event times in the enrolled cohort through H_\ell. The futility calculation imputes outstanding event times among enrolled participants and generates outcomes for the remaining participants up to N_{\max}, all through H_F. Already observed events remain fixed. Imputation uses event times, including for binary analyses; independently imputed Bernoulli outcomes at different horizons are not used.

Each completed cohort is analyzed using the prespecified method. A Bayesian analysis returns the posterior probability of its alternative; a frequentist analysis returns 1-p for the specified test. Write these scores as s^{\mathrm{now}}_{\ell m} and s^{\max}_{\ell m}. For c= prob_ha, the predictive probabilities are

\widehat P_\ell = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M} I(s^{\mathrm{now}}_{\ell m}>c), \qquad \widehat P_{\max,\ell} = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M} I(s^{\max}_{\ell m}>c).

prior_surv supplies the predictive hazard priors. For method = "bayes-surv", each completed-data analysis forms a fresh posterior using prior_surv_final and the completed cohort. It does not use the predictive posterior as a new prior, which would count the observed information twice. For method = "bayes-bin", the completed endpoint indicators are analyzed with prior_bin; the Gamma model supplies the imputation. prior_surv_final also governs hazard-based imputation at the actual final analysis when requested.

The optional horizon_settings data frame specifies horizon-specific h0, rmst_tau, or prior_bin. Without overrides, the common null value and beta prior are used at every horizon, while the RMST restriction equals the endpoint horizon. This allows, for example, different single-arm performance goals at different endpoint times. The analysis method and alternative direction remain common across horizons.

The success and futility probabilities integrate over their respective posteriors. Draw number m from one data cut is not a shared latent event trajectory with draw number m from another data cut. In contrast, the underlying simulated trial histories used to evaluate eventual outcomes are shared across horizons.

Stopping and final analysis

At look \ell, the thresholds are Q_\ell= Qn, S_\ell= Sn, and F_\ell= Fn, with Q_\ell\ge S_\ell. The first applicable rule is used.

Condition Decision Endpoint and subsequent analysis
\widehat P_\ell>Q_\ell Immediate success Declare success at H_\ell without a required final analysis
S_\ell<\widehat P_\ell\le Q_\ell Expected success Stop accrual; analyze the enrolled cohort at H_\ell after endpoint ascertainment
\widehat P_\ell\le S_\ell and \widehat P_{\max,\ell}<F_\ell Binding futility Stop and classify the adaptive trial as unsuccessful
Otherwise Continue Reach the next scheduled look, or enroll to maximum N and analyze at H_F

All comparisons are strict. Qn = 1 disables immediate success, Sn = 1 disables expected-success stopping, and Fn = 0 or NULL disables futility. The Monte Carlo bounds in a trace are diagnostics and do not replace the point estimates in these comparisons.

Figure 2. The stopping sequence for a prespecified schedule. Futility is evaluated only when enabled and neither success rule applies. The diagram describes the decisions reconstructed by apply_horizon_rules() as well as direct simulation. Complete-path simulation evaluates all planned looks regardless of these hypothetical decisions.

An expected-success stop at H_\ell fixes the endpoint for that cohort. Failure at its subsequent final analysis does not reopen the trial at a later endpoint. The futility probability concerns the final analysis at N_{\max} and H_F; it is not the probability of declaring success at any remaining interim under the entire adaptive policy.

Final analysis with dropout follows the existing method-specific choices for imputed_final. With FALSE, survival analyses retain right-censoring, while binary analyses exclude participants without complete endpoint status. With TRUE, supported methods impute missing endpoint outcomes. Independent dropout does not by itself make complete-case binary analysis unbiased. These choices and the restrictions on log-rank and Farrington-Manning final imputation are described in the technical methods vignette.

Shared histories, dropout, and timing

Event times and dropout times are generated once per simulated trial through followup_horizon. Final cohort data are re-censored at each endpoint; changing the endpoint does not redraw either process. generation_cutpoints and the arm-specific generating hazards must describe the entire collection period, and need not match the analysis partition.

If the arm-specific dropout probability is q_z by reference time H_D, then

D_i\mid Z_i=z \sim \operatorname{Exponential}(\eta_z),\qquad \eta_z=-\log(1-q_z)/H_D.

Here, H_D= dropout_horizon. This hazard remains fixed across endpoint times. The probability of dropout by the collection horizon is 1-\exp(-\eta_z H_C); the proportion actually censored by dropout can be smaller because events may occur first.

Trial results distinguish the endpoint attached to the stopping cohort from continued collection through H_C:

Selected-endpoint measure Continued-collection measure Meaning
analysis_ready_time collection_ready_time Latest observed event or censoring availability, no earlier than accrual stop
planned_completion_time planned_collection_time Accrual-stop time plus the corresponding planned horizon
followup_person_time collection_person_time Total observed event-free follow-up through the corresponding horizon

The collection measures concern the enrolled cohort, including after an early stop. They do not imply that further participants are recruited. Events or dropout can make observed follow-up end before planned completion. decision_time is the look date for immediate success or futility, and the analysis-ready date when a final analysis determines success. Administrative data-cleaning delays are not modeled.

Reusing trial paths for calibration

sim_horizon_paths() retains current-cohort predictive scores at every planned look and supported horizon, maximum-cohort predictive scores at H_F, and final analyses for every cohort and horizon. apply_horizon_rules() selects the evidence for a candidate schedule and applies its thresholds. Saving the individual scores, rather than only a predictive probability at one prob_ha, permits recalibration of the completed-data threshold as well.

Reuse can change the nondecreasing success-horizon schedule within the retained looks and horizons, and Fn, Sn, Qn, and prob_ha. The generating scenario, collection and final horizons, dropout model, analysis method, priors, horizon-specific analysis settings, maximum sample size, look sizes, and Monte Carlo counts remain fixed. Changes to those assumptions require new paths.

Direct simulation with sim_horizon_trials() skips unreached interim calculations. With the same seed, settings, and full set of endpoint_horizons, it agrees with complete-path simulation followed by rule application. Explicit seeds preserve the caller’s random-number state, and trial_offset supports consecutive batches. Changing the retained set of horizons changes the allocation of random numbers. Saved settings and calculation failures remain part of the path object when it is written with saveRDS().

The ordinary futility measure is \Pr(\text{binding futility}) under the simulated scenario. The counterfactual measure is

\Pr\{\text{binding futility and final success at }N_{\max},H_F\}.

The latter is a joint probability over simulated trials, not a conditional probability among futility stops and not the net loss of power. It is reported as futility_and_success_at_max, separately from stop_futility. A failed counterfactual final analysis makes the joint outcome unavailable for a futility trial; available and missing comparison counts accompany its summary. Failures needed to determine the candidate’s actual adaptive outcome exclude that trial and are reported separately.

Type I error must be assessed for the full adaptive design under the relevant joint null scenarios across endpoints. Overall success can occur at an earlier endpoint, so it does not necessarily constitute rejection of the final-horizon null alone. Compare candidates using paired trial-level outcomes from shared paths, and validate selected settings using independent simulations. N_trials controls operating-characteristic precision; N_impute and, where used, N_mcmc also affect the implemented stopping procedure. Calibrating stopping rules from complete trial paths gives further guidance on comparisons and Monte Carlo uncertainty.
